The Pitt's India Act (1784) unified British administration by placing the Governor General in a position of supreme authority over the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras, ensuring a centrally coordinated colonial administration.

Further Insights:

• The Act introduced a dual system: Board of Control (British government) and Court of Directors (East India Company).

• It enhanced centralization by making the Governor General dominant in civil and military matters.

• Presidencies could no longer act independently in foreign or political affairs.

• Option (1) is incorrect because the Act restricted, not expanded, presidential independence.

• Option (2) is incorrect: the Court of Directors was not dissolved; it continued with reduced powers.

• Option (4) is incorrect because civil - military departmental merger was not the Act's objective.

• The Act aimed to curb Company misgovernance after events like the Bengal famine and political scandals.

• It brought British India under direct oversight of the British government.

• The Governor General of Bengal now acted effectively as the Governor General of India in practice.

• The Act marked the beginning of structured imperial governance in India.

• It laid administrative foundations followed until the Charter Acts of the 19th century.

During the 15th century, the Sisodia dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Mewar, one of the most powerful Rajput states. The dynasty consolidated its authority under rulers such as Rana Kumbha, who significantly expanded and fortified Mewar.

Further Insights:

• The Sisodias are one of the oldest and most prominent Rajput lineages.

• Their political centre was Chittorgarh, later Udaipur.

• The 15th century saw the reign of Rana Kumbha, noted for military expansion and architectural achievements.

• Option (1) Gujarat was ruled by the Gujarat Sultanate, not Sisodias.

• Option (2) Malwa was under the Malwa Sultanate, particularly rulers like Hoshang Shah.

• Option (4) Bengal was governed by the Bengal Sultanate, not Rajput houses.

• Mewar resisted repeated invasions from neighbouring Sultanates.

• The Sisodia polity emphasized kinship-based leadership and martial autonomy.

• Mewar emerged as a stronghold of Rajput identity and valor.

• The dynasty patronized art, music, and temple construction, including the Kumbhalgarh Fort.

• The Sisodias maintained a tradition of refusing matrimonial alliances with Mughals, unlike other Rajput houses.

India challenged Pakistan's shift from a Positive List to a Negative List for Indian imports under SAFTA, arguing it violated the agreement's trade-liberalization commitments. However, Article 23 of SAFTA does not permit unilateral tariff reservations due to political disagreement, making the Reason incorrect.

Further Insights:

• Pakistan's move replaced a Positive List (allowed goods) with a Negative List (prohibited items).

• India considered this inconsistent with SAFTA's progressive trade-liberalization mandate.

• SAFTA emphasizes tariff reduction, not expansion of restrictions.

• Statement A is correct because India formally objected to the policy change.

• Article 23 relates to dispute settlement procedures, not unilateral tariff reservations.

• Therefore, the Reason (R) misinterprets SAFTA provisions.

• Statement R is false because SAFTA does not allow exemptions based on political disagreements.

• SAFTA aims to enhance economic cooperation among South Asian countries.

• Pakistan's deviation slowed the intended formation of a South Asian Free Trade Area.

• India argued that the negative list undermined market access commitments.

• The controversy highlighted broader Indo - Pak trade frictions within regional frameworks.

Article 32 grants the right to constitutional remedies, enabling citizens to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called it the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.

Further Insights:

• Article 32 empowers issuance of writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto.

• It guarantees direct access to the Supreme Court.

• It ensures effective protection of Fundamental Rights.

• Option (2) is incorrect: Article 226 empowers High Courts and also covers non-FR matters.

• Option (3) Article 21 covers the right to life and liberty, not remedies.

• Option (4) Article 14 ensures equality but does not enforce rights.

• Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right.

• Suspended only during National Emergency (except for Article 21 rights).

• It forms the backbone of judicial review.

• Ensures accountability of the State in rights violations.

• Strengthens India's constitutional democracy.

Both statements are correct: the Rajya Sabha is a continuing house that cannot be dissolved, and its members serve six-year staggered terms, with one-third retiring every two years, ensuring continuity in parliamentary functioning.

Further Insights:

• Statement 1 is correct: Rajya Sabha is permanent, unlike the Lok Sabha.

• It continues irrespective of political events such as no-confidence motions or emergencies.

• Statement 2 is correct: members serve six-year terms with biennial rotation.

• One-third of seats are vacated every two years to maintain institutional continuity.

• Rajya Sabha members are elected by state legislative assemblies through proportional representation.

• The continuing nature ensures stability in law-making, especially constitutional amendments.

• The chamber represents the federal structure of India.

• It prevents abrupt changes in legislation due to Lok Sabha dissolutions.

• The Council of Ministers remains accountable primarily to the Lok Sabha, not Rajya Sabha.

• Its composition helps maintain federal balance within Parliament.

• Rajya Sabha includes nominated members for contributions in arts, science, literature, and social service.

Auroras occur due to the interaction between charged particles from the solar wind and the Earth's magnetic field, which funnels these particles toward the poles. Their collision with atmospheric gases produces glowing lights.

Further Insights:

• Solar wind contains electrons and protons emitted by the Sun.

• The magnetosphere channels particles toward polar regions.

• Collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen, producing visible colours.

• Option (1) earthquake waves do not affect the atmosphere.

• Option (2) lightning is local electrical discharge, unrelated to auroras.

• Option (4) volcanic ash cannot produce polar light phenomena.

• Auroras appear as Aurora Borealis (north) and Aurora Australis (south).

• The colours depend on gas type and excitation energy.

• Increased auroral activity occurs during solar storms.

• Auroras help study space weather and magnetic disturbances.

• Satellites and power grids may be affected by severe geomagnetic storms.

The New Economic Policy (NEP) 1991 abolished industrial licensing for most industries, ending the Licence Raj, making the Assertion true. The Reason is false because licensing was not re-imposed; instead, policies encouraged greater competition and private-sector participation.

Further Insights:

• NEP 1991 promoted liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation.

• Industrial licensing remained only for a few sectors like defence and hazardous industries.

• The move aimed to reduce bureaucratic control and encourage competition.

• Statement R is false: licensing was not reinstated to curb monopolies.

• Monopolies were regulated through the MRTP Act, not licensing reimposition.

• The policy allowed foreign investment and technology inflow.

• Ending licensing helped improve industrial growth.

• The reform dismantled the Licence Raj system that hindered businesses.

• Industrial capacity no longer required prior government permission.

• NEP expanded India's market-oriented economic structure.

• Licensing removal improved ease of doing business.

Harvinder Singh, the Indian para-archer, became the first para archer to receive the Padma Shri after winning a historic gold medal at the 2024 Paris Paralympics. His achievement marked a major milestone in Indian para sports.

Further Insights:

• Harvinder Singh won gold in men's recurve archery at the 2024 Paralympics.

• He made history as India's first Paralympic gold medallist in archery.

• He became the first para archer ever to be honoured with the Padma Shri.

• Option (1) Rakesh Kumar is a compound para archer but not the 2024 gold medallist.

• Option (3) Mariyappan Thangavelu is a Paralympic high-jumper, not an archer.

• Option (4) Sumit Antil competes in javelin throw, not archery.

• Harvinder had earlier won a bronze in Tokyo 2020, marking India's first Paralympic archery medal.

• He is known for his strong mental resilience and precision under pressure.

• His victory significantly boosted the profile of para archery in India.

• Harvinder trains using scientific and biomechanical methods to refine technique.

• His achievements highlight India's growing strength in multi-disciplinary para sports.

In Haryana, Ragani is a prominent style of folk song, widely performed in local theatre and cultural gatherings. Despite its name, it has no connection to the classical Raga - Ragini system.

Further Insights:

• Ragani is central to Haryana's Swang (folk theatre) tradition.

• The style involves narrative, high-energy recitation, often on social or heroic themes.

• It does not follow the Raga - Ragini melodic framework.

• Option (1) is incorrect: seasonal songs (fasli geet) follow agricultural cycles.

• Option (2) is incorrect: marriage songs (shaadi geet) are ceremonial, not Ragani-style.

• Option (4) is incorrect: lullabies (loris) are soft and melodic, unlike Ragani's forceful delivery.

• Ragani uses strong poetic metre and dramatic expression.

• Instruments like dholak and harmonium accompany performances.

• Folk poet Pandit Lakhmi Chand significantly popularized Ragani.

• Ragani is often performed at melas, fairs, and community gatherings.

• The style preserves oral storytelling within Haryanvi cultural identity.

· Statement 1 is Correct: In Nagara (North Indian) architecture, the Amalaka is the segmented stone disc that crowns the main tower (Shikhara).

· Statement 2 is Incorrect: In Dravida (South Indian) architecture, the Vimana is the pyramid-like tower above the main shrine. The large gateway tower at the entrance is distinct and called the Gopuram.

Further Insights:

· Three Main Styles: Indian temples are broadly classified into Nagara (North India), Dravida (South India), and Vesara (Mixed/Hybrid style found in the Deccan).

· The Main Tower: In the North, the curvilinear tower over the deity is called the Shikhara, while in the South, the pyramidal tower is called the Vimana.

· The Crown: Nagara temples are topped by an Amalaka (ribbed stone disc) and a Kalasha (pot), whereas Dravida vimanas are topped by a dome-shaped stone called a Stupi or Shikhara.

· The Gateway: Gopurams are the massive, ornate entrance towers specific to the Dravida style; Nagara temples usually lack boundary walls and grand gateways.

· Panchayatana Style: A common layout where a main shrine is surrounded by four smaller subsidiary shrines (e.g., Kandariya Mahadeva in Khajuraho).

· Famous Examples:

o Nagara: Sun Temple (Konark) and Kandariya Mahadeva (Khajuraho).

o Dravida: Brihadeeswarar Temple (Thanjavur) and Meenakshi Temple (Madurai).

o Vesara: Virupaksha Temple (Pattadakal) and Hoysala temples (Belur/Halebidu).

· Mandapa: Both styles feature a pillared hall called a Mandapa in front of the sanctum for public assembly.

Sleeping on Jupiter was written by Anuradha Roy, an acclaimed Indian novelist whose work was longlisted for the 2015 Booker Prize. The novel addresses trauma, memory, and the contradictions of society through interwoven narrative perspectives.

Further Insights:

• Anuradha Roy is known for her lyrical prose and socially engaged themes.

• Sleeping on Jupiter examines violence, religious hypocrisy, and human resilience.

• The novel gained international recognition through its Booker longlisting.

• Option (1) Kiran Desai authored The Inheritance of Loss, the 2006 Booker winner.

• Option (3) Jhumpa Lahiri wrote works like Interpreter of Maladies and The Lowland.

• Option (4) T.N. Ninan is a noted journalist, not a Booker-listed novelist.

• Roy's fiction often blends emotional depth with social commentary.

• The book's setting includes the fictional town of Jarmuli, exploring spiritual tourism.

• Themes include childhood trauma and the search for safety and identity.

• Anuradha Roy has other notable novels including An Atlas of Impossible Longing.

• Her writing has been translated widely, reflecting her global literary appeal.

The Dumhal dance of Kashmir is uniquely performed by Wattal men, who dance in a procession around a banner or pole planted into the ground, accompanied by rhythmic singing and drums.

Further Insights:

• Dumhal is linked to the Wattal (Watal) community of Kashmir.

• Performed exclusively by men, making it socially distinctive.

• The dance begins with planting a ceremonial banner into the earth.

• Option (1) is incorrect: women do not perform Dumhal.

• Option (2) is incorrect: it uses drums and chorus singing, not solo string music.

• Option (4) is incorrect: the dance is restricted to the Wattal community, not open to all.

• Performers wear long robes and conical caps decorated with beads.

• Songs narrate folk legends and spiritual traditions.

• The banner symbolises community identity and ritual significance.

• Dumhal is performed during special cultural and religious occasions.

• It is an important marker of Kashmiri folk heritage.

An indifference curve shows all combinations of two goods that provide the consumer equal satisfaction or utility. Every point on the curve represents a consumption bundle yielding identical utility levels.

Further Insights:

• Indifference curves belong to consumer choice theory in microeconomics.

• They slope downward, reflecting trade-offs between goods.

• Higher curves represent higher utility.

• Option (2) budget constraint shows affordability, not equal satisfaction.

• Option (3) isoquant is used in production theory, not consumer theory.

• Option (4) marginal cost curve relates to cost structure of firms.

• Indifference curves are typically convex, indicating diminishing MRS.

• The slope measures marginal rate of substitution (MRS).

• They never intersect, preserving consistency of preferences.

• The entire map forms the consumer's preference structure.

• Utility is ordinal, meaning curves reflect ranked preferences, not quantity.

The Minimum Needs Programme (MNP) was introduced in the Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974 - 79) to improve access to essential services such as health, education, water supply, and nutrition for the poorer sections of society.

Further Insights:

• MNP targeted basic human development needs.

• It included components like rural health, elementary education, and nutrition.

• Introduced to address regional and social disparities.

• Option (1) Third Plan focused more on agriculture and industry.

• Option (2) Fourth Plan emphasized growth with stability, not MNP.

• Option (4) Sixth Plan addressed poverty alleviation under a new strategy.

• MNP laid foundations for later schemes like National Rural Health Mission.

• It strengthened infrastructure in rural areas.

• MNP sought to increase minimum living standards nationwide.

• The programme complemented poverty reduction objectives.

• It became part of the core development strategy in later plans.

Tamasha is a traditional folk theatre form predominantly associated with Maharashtra, combining music, dance, satire, and dramatic dialogue. It evolved as a popular rural entertainment medium with strong performative traditions.

Further Insights:

• Tamasha is rooted in Maharashtrian rural culture.

• It features lively songs (lavani) and dance sequences.

• The form includes social satire and improvisational dialogue.

• Option (1) Kerala is known for Kathakali and Koodiyattam, not Tamasha.

• Option (2) Karnataka has Yakshagana, distinct from Tamasha.

• Option (4) Odisha hosts Jatra, not Tamasha.

• Tamasha troupes are traditionally known as phad.

• Women performers often specialise in lavani, a central element of Tamasha.

• It historically provided commentary on social and political issues.

• The form integrates dholki, halgi, and sheat as musical accompaniment.

• Tamasha influenced later Marathi theatre and cinema.

In standard relay events, the baton exchange zone approved by World Athletics is 20 meters long. The baton must be passed entirely within this segment for the exchange to be valid.

Further Insights:

• The 20 m exchange zone is strictly regulated across all competitive tracks.

• Exchanges outside the zone lead to immediate disqualification.

• The full takeover zone is 30 m, but only 20 m constitutes the legal exchange area.

• Option (1) is incorrect: 10 m has never been an official exchange length.

• Option (2) is incorrect: 15 m is not part of any recognized relay rule.

• Option (4) is incorrect because 30 m refers to the total takeover zone, not the exchange segment.

• Athletes use techniques like upsweep, downsweep, and push pass within the zone.

• Proper acceleration timing is essential for optimal baton transfers.

• Officials monitor foot placement and baton position during exchange.

• Relay rules ensure uniformity and fairness across global competition.

• Effective use of the 20 m zone significantly impacts overall team timing.

By mid-2025, Odisha became the first Indian state to notify all its wetlands under the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, marking a major step in ecological protection and sustainable management.

Further Insights:

• Odisha mapped and notified almost all wetlands, including large and small ones.

• The initiative strengthens legal protection against encroachment and pollution.

• It enhances monitoring through wetland authorities and scientific assessments.

• Option (1) Kerala has major wetlands but was not the first to notify all.

• Option (3) Madhya Pradesh has extensive wetlands but lacked complete notification.

• Option (4) Himachal Pradesh has fewer wetlands and was not first to achieve this milestone.

• Wetland notification ensures zoning and regulatory oversight.

• It supports conservation of species in areas like Chilika Lake.

• Aligns with Ramsar Convention commitments on sustainable wetland use.

• Odisha's leadership sets a model for other states.

• The effort aids climate resilience, flood control, and groundwater recharge.

The Washington Consensus is a set of economic policy recommendations promoting market-oriented reforms. Export subsidies do not form part of this framework; instead, the model favours reducing distortions in trade and markets.

Further Insights:

• Washington Consensus supports trade liberalisation.

• It emphasises fiscal discipline and tax reform.

• It promotes privatisation and deregulation.

• Option (3) is correct because export subsidies distort trade, contrary to the Consensus.

• Option (1) trade liberalisation is a key component.

• Option (2) fiscal discipline is central to its macroeconomic philosophy.

• Option (4) tax reform encourages broadening the tax base.

• The framework was influential in Latin American and developing economies.

• It supports competitive exchange rates, not protectionism.

• The model encourages foreign investment openness.

• Export subsidies contradict its aim for market neutrality.

In the Gupta administration, Adeya referred to a tax or dues "to be surrendered" or given to the state/king. It is derived from the Sanskrit word Ad (to take/eat) or Da (to give), implying a fiscal obligation.

Vaishthika (Incorrect): This is related to Vishti, which was forced labor, not an enjoyment tax.

Bhāga (Incorrect): Bhāga was the King's share of the produce (usually 1/6th), which was the primary land revenue. It was not a labor levy.

Dasaparadha (Incorrect): This refers to fines imposed for the "Ten Sins" or ten specific offenses (like theft, violence, adultery, etc.), not a grain tithe.

Further Insights:

· Bhaga: The most important source of revenue, representing the King's share of the agricultural produce (usually 1/6th).

· Vishti: Refers to forced labor that the state could extract from people, considered a form of tax paid in labor.

· Hiranya: A tax explicitly paid in cash (likely gold coins) rather than in crops/kind.

· Agrahara: Land grants given to Brahmins or religious institutions, which were typically tax-free.

· Mahasandhivigrahika: The title for the Minister of War and Peace (essentially a Foreign Minister). The famous court poet Harisena held this title under Samudragupta.

· Bhukti & Vishaya: The empire was divided into provinces called Bhuktis (ruled by Uparikas) and districts called Vishayas (ruled by Vishayapatis).

· Kumaramatyas: A high-ranking cadre of officials (like modern IAS officers) who managed administration at the provincial and district levels.

The first SAF Games (now South Asian Games) were indeed held in Kathmandu, Nepal, in 1984, but not all seven SAARC nations participated. Statement 2 is incorrect because Sri Lanka, not India, has hosted the Games the most times up to 2016.

Further Insights:

• Statement 1 is partly correct in fact: the event was held in Kathmandu in 1984.

• However, only five nations participated initially, not all seven SAARC members.

• Thus, statement 1 is considered correct regarding the venue and year.

• Statement 2 is incorrect because Sri Lanka has hosted the Games more frequently than India.

• India has hosted the SAF Games three times (1987, 1995, 2016).

• Sri Lanka hosted four times (1991, 2006, 2019, plus earlier editions).

• The Games promote regional sports cooperation among South Asian nations.

• The SAF Games later became the South Asian Games.

• Early editions faced logistical and political constraints, affecting participation.

• The Games feature athletics, aquatics, and multiple team sports.

• India typically leads the overall medal tally in most editions.

A pawn may promote to any piece except the king or pawn upon reaching the opponent's back rank, making Statement 1 correct. Promotion is not restricted to previously captured pieces, making Statement 2 incorrect.

Further Insights:

• Pawn promotion allows choosing queen, rook, bishop, or knight, regardless of captured pieces.

• This rule enables multiple queens or duplicates of any piece during a game.

• Statement 1 aligns with official FIDE rules of chess.

• Statement 2 is incorrect because promotion is unlimited by material availability.

• The concept is known as "underpromotion" when promoting to rook, bishop, or knight instead of a queen.

• Promotion occurs upon reaching the 8th rank (White) or 1st rank (Black).

• The promoted piece is immediately active, altering the game's tactical landscape.

• Pawn promotion is crucial in endgame strategy.

• Chess notation denotes promotion with =Q, =R, =B, or =N.

• Historically, older chess variants restricted promotion, but modern chess does not.

• Promotion removes the pawn permanently; it does not remain a pawn afterward.

Statements 1 and 2 are correct regarding tendons and ligaments, but statement 3 is incorrect because cartilage does not contain calcium salts; bone does. Thus, cartilage is softer, not harder, than bone.

Further Insights:

• Statement 1 is correct: tendons attach muscle to bone and are made of dense regular connective tissue.

• Statement 2 is correct: ligaments connect bone to bone and have slight elasticity.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the correct option: He spoke so ____ that the audience was mesmerized.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Chapter and verse
questions.questionHtml:
Choose the correct meaning of idiom:

questions.solution:
The idiom chapter and verse means providing information with exact details, specific references, or full authority.

Option (1) Half-formed reasoning conveys incomplete thought, which is unrelated.

Option (2) Incomplete explanation is the opposite of the idiom's meaning.

Option (4) Analogy or example does not capture precision or authoritative detail.

She quoted the policy chapter and verse to support her argument, refusing the vague and incomplete explanations given by others.

questions.question: Find the correctly spelled word meaning for extreme frugality.

Usage example:

His parsimonious habits bordered on extreme frugality, while his wealthy brother was anything but miserly.

questions.question: A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech. The patient said, "It has been three days since I last slept."
questions.questionHtml:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

The patient said, "It has been three days since I last slept."

options.text: The patient said that it was three days since he last slept.
options.html: The patient said that it was three days since he last slept.

options.text: The patient said that it had been three days since he had last slept.
options.html: The patient said that it had been three days since he had last slept.

options.text: The patient said that he didn't sleep for three days.
options.html: The patient said that he didn't sleep for three days.

options.text: The patient said that he was not sleeping for three days.
options.html: The patient said that he was not sleeping for three days.

questions.solution:
Present perfect (has been) changes to past perfect (had been) in indirect speech.

"I" becomes he and "I last slept" becomes he had last slept to maintain the sequence of tenses.

This preserves both duration and time reference accurately.

Why other options are wrong:

1) Uses was, which changes the meaning.

3) "didn't sleep for three days" alters the sense and structure.

4) "was not sleeping" is a continuous form not present in the original.

Correct Indirect speech:

The patient said that it had been three days since he had last slept.

questions.question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'A harmless, inert substance or pill prescribed more for psychological benefit than for any physiological effect'.
questions.questionHtml: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'A harmless, inert substance or pill prescribed more for psychological benefit than for any physiological effect'.
questions.solution:
Placebo is an inactive substance given to satisfy a patient's expectation without real physiological effect.

Option (1) Panacea means a cure-all.

Option (3) Antidote counteracts poison.

Option (4) Palliative relieves symptoms without curing the disease.

Usage example:

The doctor administered a placebo to test psychological response, whereas a real antidote would have been required for actual toxicity.

questions.questionHtml: According to the passage, what complicates gender oppression further for rural women?
questions.solution:
The passage emphasizes intersectionality - gender oppression becomes worse when combined with caste, class, and religion. A Dalit woman faces multiple layers of marginalization, not just gender-based discrimination.

Why other options are wrong:

1) Internet access is not a factor described.

2) Urban migration is not mentioned.

4) Western education is not shown to worsen oppression.

questions.question: What long-term solution does the author propose to resolve gender inequality?
questions.questionHtml: What long-term solution does the author propose to resolve gender inequality?
questions.solution:
The author argues that laws alone cannot undo cultural conditioning. Real change requires pedagogical reform, including dismantling gender essentialism from childhood and promoting inclusive gender norms. This is framed as a long-term cultural shift.

Why other options are wrong:

1) Laws are insufficient on their own.

3) Arranged marriages are irrelevant.

4) Reservations are not the main proposed solution.

questions.question: A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech. Teacher said, "Who broke the window?"
questions.questionHtml:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

Teacher said, "Who broke the window?"

options.text: Teacher asked who had broken the window.
options.html: Teacher asked who had broken the window.

options.text: Teacher asked who has broken the window.
options.html: Teacher asked who has broken the window.

options.text: Teacher asked who did break the window.
options.html: Teacher asked who did break the window.

options.text: Teacher said who broke the window.
options.html: Teacher said who broke the window.

questions.solution:
The reporting verb said changes to asked because it is a question.

Direct question in simple past (broke) changes to past perfect (had broken) in indirect speech.

No question mark is used in indirect form.

Why other options are wrong:

2) Uses has broken, which is incorrect after a past reporting verb.

3) Uses emphatic form did break, incorrect for indirect speech.

4) Retains direct form without converting to a question structure.

Correct Indirect speech:

Teacher asked who had broken the window.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: CADAVEROUS
questions.questionHtml: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: CADAVEROUS
questions.solution:
Cadaverous means extremely thin, gaunt, or death-like in appearance. The closest meaning is pale, which conveys a lifeless, bloodless look.

Option (1) Vibrant means energetic and colorful, opposite of cadaverous.

Option (3) Lively also conveys energy and animation, which is contrary to a death-like state.

Option (4) Healthy suggests robustness, which is again the opposite of cadaverous.

Usage example:

The cadaverous man looked so pale that even the usually vibrant crowd fell silent, unsure whether he was healthy or deathly ill.
